strengths: Proposes a clear role-based agentic workflow (Planner, Grounder, Verifier, Answerer) for temporal-grounded long-video reasoning, with each role addressing a distinct sub-problem.

Introduces Chain-of-LoRA to switch among role-specific LoRA adapters on a single base MLLM, achieving the performance of multiple distributed models with much lower GPU memory (4.2G vs 16.6G in Table 9).
Extensive empirical evaluation on 14 benchmarks across grounded VideoQA, video temporal grounding, and general video QA, with strong results on several long-video benchmarks.
Detailed ablations study the contribution of individual roles, verifier design, temporal feature pyramid, auxiliary losses, and different integration strategies.
Provides implementation details, prompt templates, and qualitative visualizations that help clarify the workflow and design.
The 2B/7B models show competitive or SOTA results against much larger open-source and closed-source baselines on several grounding and long-video QA tasks.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the planner/grounder/verifier/answerer workflow is closely related to prior agentic video understanding frameworks, and Chain-of-LoRA is primarily an efficient engineering adaptation rather than a fundamentally new reasoning algorithm.

The paper overclaims an MCTS-based approach in the related work, but the actual method is top-N candidate generation plus verifier reranking; there is no tree search, rollout, or backpropagation, so the connection to MCTS is misleading.

Some central claims are overstated. For example, on CG-Bench the 7B model does not surpass GPT-4o in long-video accuracy (38.4 vs 45.2) but does surpass it on some grounding metrics; the paper should state this precisely. Similarly, on ReXTime the zero-shot model surpasses fine-tuned variants only on QA accuracy, not on grounding metrics.

The mathematical formulation of the boundary regression loss appears to contain a typo (using b_i^s - \hat{b}_i^e instead of \hat{b}_i^s), and verifier confidence calibration via teacher-forced likelihoods is not deeply analyzed.
Evaluation lacks statistical significance tests or error bars, which is important for claims of SOTA across many benchmarks.

Although reproducibility is partially supported through implementation details and prompts, no code or model release is mentioned, and some data-generation details (e.g., verifier training labels from GPT-4o mini) are under-specified.

The general VideoQA results are mixed: the models improve on some long-video benchmarks but still lag GPT-4o on Video-MME overall and long subsets, so the claimed broad superiority should be tempered.

strengths: The paper conducts a broad empirical evaluation across 14 benchmarks and three task families (grounded video QA, video temporal grounding, general video QA), which is substantially more extensive than many comparable submissions.

The role-based workflow (Planner, Grounder, Verifier, Answerer) is intuitive and aligns with human-like video reasoning; the qualitative example and ablation studies help illustrate the intended behavior.

The Chain-of-LoRA mechanism offers a practical parameter-efficient way to switch among role-specific behaviors without duplicating the base model, and the reported memory reduction versus the all-distributed setting is a reasonable engineering advantage.

The Grounder's timestamp decoder and the Verifier's reranking strategy produce strong zero-shot temporal grounding results on several benchmarks, and the 2B model is surprisingly competitive on some long-video tasks.
The paper includes useful implementation details, prompt templates, and additional ablations in the appendix, which improves transparency to some degree.
weaknesses: The central state-of-the-art claims are overstated and sometimes contradicted by the paper's own tables. For example, on CG-Bench the abstract/introduction imply VideoMind surpasses GPT-4o on long-video grounded QA, but Table 2 shows GPT-4o achieves 45.2 long-acc while VideoMind-2B/7B achieve only 31.0/38.4. Similarly, Table 5 shows VideoMind is well below GPT-4o/Gemini on Video-MME, and Table 6 does not surpass fine-tuned temporal grounding specialists.

The paper repeatedly claims or implies a video moment-level MCTS approach (Section 2.3), but the actual inference algorithm is candidate generation followed by verification and reranking; there is no tree search, rollouts, or MCTS optimization. This is a serious unsupported central claim.

The novelty is limited. Role decomposition for video agents and multi-LoRA role conditioning are not fundamentally new; Chain-of-LoRA is essentially serving multiple role-specific LoRA adapters on a shared backbone. The paper does not adequately differentiate its approach from prior video-agent works such as SeViLA, LLoVi, VideoAgent, etc.

The evaluation is not consistently apples-to-apples. Zero-shot and fine-tuned baselines are mixed, model sizes differ greatly, and some claimed wins are selective (e.g., ReXTime grounding metrics are lower than fine-tuned VTimeLLM despite the text claiming superiority over fine-tuned variants). The TACoS experiment also uses data that was already in Grounder pretraining, making comparisons to fine-tuned specialists less clean.

Several reported gains are marginal and may not support strong conclusions. For instance, the Planner ablation improves ReXTime accuracy from 69.2 to 70.0, and other role contributions are often within 0.1-0.8 points, without significance testing or variance estimates.

Reproducibility is weak. The construction of Planner and Verifier training data is only partially described, the full data mixture is large and complex, and no code/model release is mentioned. This makes it difficult to verify the results or reproduce the agent behavior.

The All-Distributed baseline is poorly justified and appears almost identical in performance to Chain-of-LoRA while using much more memory; it is unclear whether this is a fair or meaningful comparison, or whether the main benefit is simply standard multi-LoRA serving rather than a novel reasoning mechanism.

strengths: Introduces a clear and well-motivated role-based agentic workflow (Planner, Grounder, Verifier, Answerer) for temporal-grounded long-video reasoning, addressing an important challenge in multimodal video understanding.

The Chain-of-LoRA strategy is an effective and practical contribution: it enables role switching via lightweight LoRA adapters on a single Qwen2-VL backbone, achieving performance comparable to a fully distributed multi-model setup while using far less GPU memory.

Extensive evaluation across 14 benchmarks covering grounded VideoQA, video temporal grounding, and general VideoQA, with strong results on several key benchmarks such as ReXTime, NExT-GQA, Charades-STA, and QVHighlights.

The paper provides useful implementation details, prompts, dataset statistics, and ablation studies (e.g., temporal feature pyramid, verifier design, auxiliary decoding loss), which support reproducibility and clarify design choices.

The 2B and 7B variants demonstrate competitive or superior performance against much larger open-source models and some closed-source models on multiple grounding-focused benchmarks, highlighting the efficiency and practical value of the approach.
weaknesses: Some claims are overstated: the paper frequently claims state-of-the-art results across all settings, but on general VideoQA benchmarks such as Video-MME, MLVU, and LVBench, VideoMind is below GPT-4o and Gemini-1.5-Pro, and on CG-Bench it does not surpass GPT-4o in long-video accuracy despite such wording in the text.

The relation to MCTS is misleading: Section 2.3 describes a 'video moment-level MCTS approach,' but the actual pipeline uses top-N candidate generation followed by verifier-based reranking, not Monte Carlo Tree Search. This should be corrected or clearly repositioned.

Novelty is incremental in parts: the framework combines existing ideas such as role-based prompting, LoRA adapters, temporal grounding heads, and verifier reranking. The individual components are not fundamentally new, even though their integration is effective.

Comparisons are not always apples-to-apples: VideoMind is sometimes evaluated zero-shot against fine-tuned temporal grounding specialists, and general VideoQA comparisons involve models with different backbone sizes, training data, and tuning budgets.

Reproducibility could be strengthened: no code or model release is mentioned, and the separate training of multiple role-specific adapters may make exact replication nontrivial despite the provided implementation details.

strengths: Proposes an integrated multi-role agentic workflow for temporal-grounded video reasoning with planner, grounder, verifier, and answerer, decomposing long-video reasoning into localization, verification, and answer synthesis.
Introduces Chain-of-LoRA, enabling efficient role switching via role-specific LoRA adapters on a shared LMM backbone, reducing memory overhead compared with deploying multiple full models.
Develops a timestamp decoder with temporal feature pyramid and specialized prediction heads, achieving strong temporal grounding performance across several benchmarks.
Conducts extensive experiments on 15 benchmarks across Grounded VideoQA, Video Temporal Grounding, and General VideoQA, with comparisons to many closed-source and open-source baselines.

Provides substantial ablation studies and analyses, including role contributions, timestamp modeling designs, feature pyramid effects, verifier designs, planner reliability, inference efficiency, and error propagation.
Offers a reproducibility statement and promises open-source code, models, datasets, and training logs, which supports future research.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the multi-role agentic pipeline and LoRA-based role switching are incremental combinations of existing ideas such as tool-use agents, multi-LoRA serving, and ActionFormer-style grounding architectures.

Several references appear irrelevant or incorrect, e.g., brain imaging/optogenetic fMRI papers cited for human video reasoning and future-dated citations, which raises concerns about citation accuracy and manuscript rigor.

Some claims are overbroad: the paper states SOTA on Charades-STA and broad superiority over GPT-4o/Gemini, but results are mixed; on Charades-STA some metrics are lower than UniTime, and on CG-Bench long-acc the 2B model is lower than GPT-4o and Gemini.
Roles are trained separately on curated datasets rather than jointly optimized, which may limit overall coordination and leaves potential error propagation insufficiently addressed.
The planner relies on pre-defined plans and synthetic query rephrasing data generated by GPT-4o mini, limiting flexibility and introducing data-construction dependence.
Some comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples: several closed-source baseline numbers are taken from other papers, and controlled experiments are limited to small minisets.

The grounder training data overlaps with some evaluation datasets (e.g., QVHighlights, TACoS), which complicates zero-shot claims and requires clearer separation between training and evaluation protocols.
The verifier uses top-5 candidates and a fixed zoom-in/boolean setup, but lacks ablation on candidate number, zoom-in ratio, and robustness to varying grounding errors.
Chain-of-LoRA is only tested on a limited set of base models and is not compared against other adapter composition or model-merging strategies.
The paper does not provide sufficiently detailed qualitative failure analysis or discuss the practical costs of maintaining multiple LoRA adapters and role-switching in diverse deployment settings.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical study across 15 benchmarks and three task families, with extensive appendix ablations and error analysis.

Chain-of-LoRA provides a practical memory-efficient way to serve multiple role-specific LoRA adapters, reducing peak memory relative to all-distributed models (4.2G vs 16.6G) with identical measured performance.
The timestamp decoder with temporal feature pyramid and multi-loss training is well motivated and shows consistent gains over alternative timestamp modeling designs in ablation.
The verifier's zoom-in and special-token boundary design improves grounding quality, and the paper reports useful reliability/error propagation analyses.
Strong reproducibility effort: code, models, datasets, logs, prompts, implementation details, and ethics statement are provided.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the paper combines existing agentic video QA, temporal grounding, LoRA, feature pyramid, and verifier ideas. Chain-of-LoRA is primarily a memory-sharing engineering trick; All-Distributed and Chain-of-LoRA achieve identical performance, so it does not improve reasoning itself.

Missing critical controls: no comparison to the base Qwen2-VL-7B (or other base models) on most benchmarks, especially General VideoQA. For 2B, gains over the base model are modest (e.g., NExT-GQA 69.6→71.4, Video-MME 53.0→55.4), and it is unclear how much of the 7B result comes from the pipeline versus the stronger backbone.

Several central claims are overstated or unsupported. The abstract/introduction claim that VideoMind-2B surpasses GPT-4o and Gemini-1.5-Pro on long video benchmarks is false in the main tables for Video-MME and CG-Bench, and in the controlled mini experiments the 2B model does not surpass Gemini-1.5-Pro on MLVU or LVBench. 'State-of-the-art' on Charades-STA is also not clearly established given ties/losses to UniTime on some metrics.

Evaluation protocols are inconsistent and potentially leaky. The planner is trained on NExT-QA and evaluated on NExT-GQA, which is derived from NExT-QA; the grounder/verifier are trained on QVHighlights/TACoS/DiDeMo and then evaluated on related benchmarks, yet the paper does not rigorously address overlap or target-set co-training. Closed-source comparisons are partly taken from prior papers rather than aligned runs.

The planner is not truly dynamic or agentic: it selects among three pre-defined plans via a trained classifier, with query rephrasing trained from GPT-4o-mini synthetic data. The claimed adaptive coordination is much weaker than presented.

Ablations are largely limited to 2B, with no equivalent 7B role ablations. The general VideoQA results are particularly hard to interpret without base-model numbers, and the controlled closed-source comparisons use only 300-sample subsets.

The MultiHop-EgoQA evaluation does not demonstrate true multi-hop reasoning; the method simply emits multiple candidate moments in one grounding step, and sentence-similarity scores are low for the 2B variant.

The paper's positioning relative to recent video agents and grounded VideoQA methods is incomplete; key alternatives and stronger task-specific baselines are missing on several benchmarks, weakening the significance claims.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: temporal-grounded video reasoning with an agentic workflow combining planning, grounding, verification, and answering.
Extensive evaluation across 15 benchmarks spanning Grounded VideoQA, Video Temporal Grounding, and General VideoQA, with many comparisons and ablations.

Chain-of-LoRA is a practical and reasonably effective mechanism for integrating multiple roles into one base model with role-specific LoRA adapters, reducing memory overhead compared with maintaining multiple full models.

The grounder design (timestamp decoder, temporal feature pyramid, boundary regression, contrastive loss) and the verifier with zoom-in and boundary special tokens show clear improvements in ablations.

Strong empirical results on several benchmarks, including QVHighlights, Charades-STA, NExT-GQA, and long-video QA settings, with 2B/7B variants outperforming much larger or closed-source baselines on selected tasks.
Good reproducibility effort: code, models, datasets, and demos are stated to be available; the appendix contains implementation details, prompts, and additional analyses.
The paper includes useful error analysis, efficiency analysis, and integration experiments with other LMMs and closed-source models, adding depth beyond standard benchmark tables.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the role-based agentic workflow and LoRA-based role switching are largely combinations of existing ideas, and the planner is restricted to a few predefined plans rather than supporting open-ended dynamic planning.

Evaluation consistency is concerning for some temporal grounding results: TACoS and QVHighlights appear in the grounder training data, yet TACoS is marked as FT ✗ with only a note that the method was co-trained on the dataset, which complicates fair comparison to fine-tuned specialists; train/val/test overlap should be explicitly clarified.

Some headline claims are selective: the paper claims superiority over GPT-4o/Gemini-1.5-Pro, but this is not true on all benchmarks, e.g., Video-MME and CG-Bench long-acc; newer closed models such as Gemini-2.5-Pro in the appendix are substantially stronger on the mini benchmarks, weakening the significance of the closed-source comparisons.
Several SOTA claims need qualification: on Charades-STA, VideoMind has lower mIoU than UniTime; on ActivityNet-Captions it is not clearly state-of-the-art; on CG-Bench long-acc it is below GPT-4o.
Query rephrasing training data is generated by GPT-4o mini without human validation, raising potential annotation bias or leakage concerns.

The memory comparison shows Chain-of-LoRA has essentially the same peak memory as the all-in-one baseline, so the efficiency advantage is mainly versus a distributed multi-model setup; latency and training/inference costs are not analyzed in depth.

Roles are trained separately and joint optimization is left for future work; possible interference among role LoRAs and error propagation in the sequential pipeline are acknowledged but not fully resolved.
